title: Dutch pension funds move from defined benefit to the new contribution-based system (Wtp)
event_date: 1 January 2026 (largest wave so far); deadline 1 January 2028
what_happened: Thirty Dutch pension funds, holding about EUR 542bn, had converted to the new system by 31 March 2026; 24 of them moved on 1 January 2026. Remaining funds must transfer accrued entitlements by 1 January 2028.
client_effect: A fund that used to promise a fixed pension now manages personal pots by age group. Younger members can take more risk and need less interest-rate protection; older members still need stable income. The fund's hedging and return portfolios have to be redesigned around age cohorts and a solidarity reserve.
decision_that_changes: How much interest-rate hedging to keep and for which cohorts; what goes into the return portfolio (more equities, credit, private assets); how the reserve is invested; whether the fiduciary manager and mandate structure still fit.
existing_investments: Long-dated swap and bond hedges can shrink for younger cohorts; existing matching mandates may be resized or re-benchmarked; reporting moves to cohort level and becomes more frequent.
possible_gsam_response: (Layer B, not a GS statement) Offer cohort-aware fixed income and return-seeking building blocks, and analysis specific to each fund's lifecycle design, rather than a generic LDI pitch. GSAM's Dutch presence since the 2022 NN IP acquisition is relevant capacity, but no public source ties a specific Wtp mandate to GSAM.
sales_angle: For funds still to convert (2027 and 2028 waves), the opening is the portfolio redesign: asking what the new return portfolio needs that the old one lacked.
rm_angle: For existing mandates, the job is to keep the mandate fit for purpose through conversion: revised guidelines, benchmarks and reporting, and honesty if a matching mandate should shrink.
risks_counterarguments: The January 2026 wave passed calmly, so the 'forced selling' story may be overdone; estimates of future hedge reduction come from interested parties and carry wide uncertainty. Some funds keep higher hedging than the market expected. Many Dutch funds delegate to fiduciary managers, so the real buyer may be the fiduciary, not the fund.
client_question: Which of your age cohorts will hold less interest-rate hedging after conversion, and what will replace it in their return portfolio?
watch: DNB quarterly counts of converted funds and assets; conversion dates of the largest remaining funds; long-end euro swap spreads around 1 January 2027 and 2028; insurer demand for long duration ahead of January 2027 Solvency II changes.
base_case: Forecast, not fact: the remaining Dutch funds convert on or before 1 January 2028 and hedging demand at the long end falls gradually, cohort by cohort, with return portfolios redesigned as they go.
alternatives: (1) Conversions are delayed and the old system's hedging persists longer. (2) Several large funds reduce hedges at the same time and long-dated euro rates move sharply.
would_change_view: The number and size of funds converting on 1 January 2027; the Dutch central bank's transition reporting; long-dated euro swap rates around conversion dates; funds' published lifecycle designs.

title: UK and EU money market fund rules: higher expected liquidity, no forced fees or gates
event_date: 8 June 2026 (FCA update); UK regime targeted end-2026
what_happened: The FCA said the Government expects to repeal the UK Money Market Funds Regulation by end-2026, with new FCA rules. Guidance will expect stable-NAV funds to hold 40% weekly liquid assets (20% for variable-NAV) and the link between liquidity thresholds and fees or gates will be removed. A European Commission report in 2026 pointed to the same 40%/20% levels as supervisory benchmarks without rewriting the EU regulation. EU-domiciled funds, about 90% of sterling MMF assets, stay on sale in the UK under an extended temporary regime pending an equivalence decision.
client_effect: A treasurer using a stable-value fund gets a fund that holds more cash-like assets and is less likely to gate in a stress, at the cost of slightly lower yield. Continued UK access to EU funds is expected but not yet permanent.
decision_that_changes: Whether to keep operating cash in LVNAV funds, move part to government-only (Public Debt CNAV) funds, or segment cash into operating, reserve and strategic buckets with short-duration strategies for the last.
existing_investments: Existing MMF holdings are unaffected day to day; yield may drift a little lower as funds hold more weekly liquidity; investment policies that reference old thresholds or 'fees and gates' triggers need updating.
possible_gsam_response: (Layer B, not a GS statement) Explain how each GS liquidity fund already sits against the new expectations, and offer cash segmentation: money market funds for daily cash, short-duration accounts for cash not needed for months.
sales_angle: Lead with resilience and reporting (for example through the Mosaic portal) rather than yield alone; most treasurers already hold several providers, so the realistic aim is a larger share of balances.
rm_angle: Review each client's investment policy against the new rules before the client asks, and flag any share class or domicile changes early.
risks_counterarguments: Final FCA rules were not published at the cutoff, and the equivalence decision could attach conditions. Balances are driven far more by interest rates and bank deposit pricing than by regulation. Fees are thin, so a small yield difference moves large balances quickly in either direction.
client_question: Does your treasury policy still refer to liquidity fees and redemption gates as triggers, and how would you want your cash split if stable-value funds yield a little less?
watch: FCA policy statement and interim guidance on weekly liquid assets; HM Treasury legislation; equivalence decision for EU MMFs (indicated for 2027); central bank rate path; industry sterling MMF assets.
base_case: Forecast, not fact: the UK replaces its inherited money market fund regulation with FCA rules on roughly the stated timetable, stable-value funds hold more weekly liquidity, and EU-domiciled funds stay available to UK investors.
alternatives: (1) The equivalence decision is delayed or conditional and UK investors face a narrower choice. (2) Higher liquidity requirements cut yields enough that treasurers move part of their cash to deposits or short-duration accounts.
would_change_view: The final FCA rules; the Treasury's equivalence decision; the yield gap between stable-value funds and bank deposits; flows between fund types reported by trade bodies.

title: Tokenised money market fund shares: collateral use, not yet a new product for treasurers
what_happened: BNY and Goldman Sachs launched a solution that records 'mirror' tokens of money market fund shares on Goldman's GS DAP ledger, with subscriptions and redemptions through BNY's LiquidityDirect and BNY remaining the official record. GSAM was among the first fund managers.
client_effect: In principle an institution could post fund shares as collateral directly instead of redeeming to cash first, keeping yield and avoiding a forced sale in stress.
decision_that_changes: For now, little: it is an operational option for institutions that post margin, not a different fund.
existing_investments: No change to existing fund holdings.
possible_gsam_response: (Layer B, not a GS statement) Be able to explain plainly what tokenisation changes (transfer and collateral use) and what it does not (the fund's assets, risk and regulation).
sales_angle: A conversation opener with derivatives users and hedge funds that post margin daily; not a reason by itself to switch provider.
rm_angle: Keep clients informed without overselling; note any availability limits by fund domicile.
risks_counterarguments: Launch coverage was US-focused; no public evidence was found on volumes or on availability for European funds or EMEA clients. Regulators in Europe have not broadly accepted tokenised fund shares as margin.
client_question: How much cash do you redeem from money market funds each month just to meet margin calls?
watch: Regulatory acceptance of tokenised MMF shares as collateral in the UK and EU; extension to European-domiciled funds; adoption figures.

title: Insurance capital rules change in 2027 (EU) and the UK loosens matching-adjustment investing
what_happened: Amended EU Solvency II rules (Directive (EU) 2025/2) take effect on 30 January 2027. In the UK, the PRA consulted in April 2025 on a Matching Adjustment Investment Accelerator that lets insurers add self-assessed eligible assets to matching-adjustment portfolios before formal approval, within the lower of 5% of liabilities or GBP 2bn and a 24-month regularisation window.
client_effect: An insurer chooses assets by yield after capital charge, not by yield alone. Rule changes alter which assets are 'capital-efficient' and how quickly an annuity writer can invest in new private asset types.
decision_that_changes: Allocation to long-dated and private credit assets; how much to outsource; which managers can structure assets to be matching-adjustment eligible.
existing_investments: Existing portfolios are re-tested against new capital charges; some long-duration and equity positions become cheaper or dearer to hold.
possible_gsam_response: (Layer B, not a GS statement) Show the capital-adjusted return of proposed assets under the client's own regulatory basis; GSAM describes 'capital-efficient investment strategies' and asset-liability advice as part of its insurance offer.
sales_angle: Sales must speak the insurer's language (capital charge, book yield, liability matching) before talking about products.
rm_angle: Relationship managers coordinate regulatory reporting data and help the client evidence eligibility of assets already held.
risks_counterarguments: The final UK policy statement and the detailed EU changes were not read in this research, so details must be checked before quoting. Regulators are also wary of private-asset concentration at annuity writers. Survey intentions to raise private assets may not turn into allocations.
client_question: Which assets in your portfolio become more or less capital-efficient under the January 2027 rules?
watch: PRA policy statement on the accelerator; EIOPA and Commission delegated acts before January 2027; insurers' reported private-asset allocations.
base_case: Forecast, not fact: capital rules in the EU and UK move modestly in the direction of making long-dated and private assets easier for insurers to hold, and insurers add them selectively.
alternatives: (1) Supervisors tighten their stance on private-asset concentration at annuity writers and allocations stall. (2) A credit event makes insurers pull back regardless of the rules.
would_change_view: The final UK policy statement and EU delegated rules; supervisory letters on private assets; insurers' reported allocations a year after survey intentions; credit losses in asset-backed finance.

title: Insurers say they will keep adding private assets (GSAM Global Insurance Survey 2026)
what_happened: GSAM's 15th annual survey of 434 insurance CIOs and CFOs found 62% plan to increase private asset allocations in 2026; asset-backed finance had the highest net intended increase (38%), then investment-grade private placements (35%) and senior direct lending (33%). 55% expect a US recession within three years, up from 46%.
client_effect: Insurers are looking for extra yield from illiquid, often investment-grade, private credit while worrying about the cycle and valuations.
decision_that_changes: How much liquidity to give up, and whether to build private credit capability in-house or outsource.
existing_investments: Public investment-grade bond portfolios may be trimmed to fund private placements; liquidity buffers need re-checking.
possible_gsam_response: (Layer B, not a GS statement) Private credit and asset-backed finance origination offered inside an insurance mandate with capital and liquidity analysis attached.
sales_angle: The survey is itself a sales and credibility tool: it gives a reason to open a conversation with a CIO using peer data.
rm_angle: Use the peer data in portfolio reviews to test, not to push, the client's current allocation.
risks_counterarguments: It is a survey run by a manager that sells these assets, and it measures intentions. No EMEA breakdown was found on the pages read. Rising recession expectations cut against adding illiquid credit.
client_question: Where does your private-asset allocation sit against your liquidity stress test, not against your peers?
watch: Next survey (around March 2027); regulator statements on private assets at insurers; default and valuation data in private credit.

title: Goldman Sachs builds onshore presence in the Gulf: Abu Dhabi, Kuwait, Riyadh regional headquarters
what_happened: Goldman Sachs announced an Abu Dhabi Global Market office in 2023, opened a Kuwait office in October 2025 and officially opened a new office and regional headquarters in Riyadh's King Abdullah Financial District in December 2025, adding to Dubai, Doha and Riyadh (since 2008). Asset and wealth management is named among its Saudi businesses.
client_effect: Gulf sovereign and public institutions increasingly expect managers to be present, licensed and hiring locally, and to offer partnerships and co-investment rather than off-the-shelf funds.
decision_that_changes: Which managers receive large strategic mandates and partnerships, and whether coverage is run from the region or from London.
existing_investments: Existing relationships may be re-papered with local entities; expectations for local servicing and knowledge transfer rise.
possible_gsam_response: (Layer B, not a GS statement) Coverage closer to clients and bespoke structures such as the US$1bn Mubadala private credit separately managed account (2024), which was run by Goldman Sachs Alternatives.
sales_angle: A small number of very large, sophisticated clients: the sale is a multi-year institutional partnership involving senior people across the firm, not a product pitch.
rm_angle: Servicing involves co-investment reporting, training and secondment-type requests as much as performance reviews.
risks_counterarguments: The office openings are firm-wide; public sources do not say which house asset-management client coverage. A 2027 Dubai CSG student role is listed, so not all Middle East coverage sits in London. Concentration risk: a handful of clients, whose priorities can shift with oil revenue and domestic spending plans.
client_question: How do you weigh a manager's local presence against its global investment platform when you award a strategic mandate?
watch: Further local licences and hires; announced sovereign partnerships; oil price and Gulf fiscal balances; domestic-investment mandates of sovereign funds.
base_case: Forecast, not fact: Gulf sovereign investors continue to reward managers that are licensed, staffed and investing locally, and prefer partnerships and co-investment to buying funds.
alternatives: (1) Lower energy revenues or domestic spending needs reduce the capital available to external managers. (2) Regional conflict or policy change makes local presence harder to sustain.
would_change_view: Oil-price-driven changes to fund deployment plans; announced partnerships and whether they are funded; licensing and headcount announcements; public statements by the funds about external-manager use.
